newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Short-selling seen making quiet debut in Malaysia.
newsitem.headline: Short-selling seen making quiet debut in Malaysia.

text.p: Come Monday, short sales of stocks will be legal in Malaysia, but fund managers and analysts don't expect a rush to bet on a slump in share prices.

After careful deliberations and the unveiling in June of a strict set of criteria, stock regulators have confined regulated short sales to 50 stocks, including some of the bluest of Malaysia's blue chips.
Short selling occurs when an investor sells securities he does not own in the hopes of buying them back at a lower price.
The practice is common in major stock markets, and is another step Malaysia is taking to liberalise its financial markets to compete with those of developed nations.

The list of 50 stocks, announced on Friday, was longer than the 20 to 30 names the exchange earlier indicated would be short-sale candidates. Banks and finance companies dominated the roster, with 13 representatives.
Besides using short-sales to bet on a downturn in stock prices, the transactions are also used to hedge portfolios.
However, short-selling is most profitable when involving volatile stocks, and blue chips, by their nature, tend to be stable in price.

"It's a move in the right direction, but basically, because the rules are rather stringent at the moment, it will certainly take some time before interest develops," said Desmond Ch'ng, an analyst with South Johor Securities.
Said another analyst, "This is a new way to trade, and I think people will take a wait-and-see attitude."

The Securities Commission said listed firms which can be sold short must have average daily market capitalisation of 2.0 billion ringgit ($800 million) for the past three months, a minimum of 2,000 registered shareholders and five years uninterrupted profit.
Even those betting on bad news to make a profit on stocks may be disappointed.

"We're at the tail-end of the results season," said Razani Radzi, research manager at PB Securities. "There's very little in terms of negative corporate surprises. You don't have a very good market to test out short sales fully."
Fund managers and dealers surveyed said they had received little to no inquiries from customers about short selling.
While welcoming the development for improving market liquidity, Robert Coombe, executive director at Commerce Asset Fund Managers said, "We're not going to get involved in the foreseeable future."
After bad experiences in the past, regulators have placed requirements that short sellers have on hand the securities for delivery in their transactions, to avoid "naked" short selling.
In 1993, eight investors in Union Paper Holdings Bhd were charged for failing to deliver the scrip for the entire amount they short-sold.
Only stockbrokers who have approved guidelines, such as apprising clients of the risks involved and ensuring they have the capacity to meet financial commitments, can participate in the transactions.

But it is some of these protections that are turning off potential short-sellers. Noting that all regulated short sales must be identified as such at the time of the order, a local fund manager said, "Why would I want to reveal my position to the market?"
